Here in this article, we show how to use the package's function `endemicMap`
to map where the species of any plant family or genus are endemic. A species
is endemic to a botanical country when it is native to that botanical country
only, following the level 3 of the
[World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions](https://www.tdwg.org/standards/wgsrpd/).
While `powoMap` shows where species occur (species richness), `endemicMap`
shows where species are restricted to, which highlights centres of endemism
and areas of conservation priority.\

\

# Setup

Install the latest development version of __expowo__ from
[GitHub](https://github.com/):

``` r
#install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("DBOSlab/expowo")
```
```{r package load, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(expowo)
```

\

# 1. Mining the species list and their distribution

`endemicMap` uses as input data the species list and their native distribution
returned by `powoSpecies`. The example below mines all accepted species of
Fabaceae. The first search downloads the data of the World Checklist of
Vascular Plants (about 90 MB) only once, so any following search takes a few
seconds.\

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fab <- powoSpecies(family = "Fabaceae",
                   verbose = FALSE)
```

\

# 2. Mapping the endemic species of a family

To map the endemic species, just provide the output of `powoSpecies` to
`endemicMap`. The function counts the species whose native distribution, in the
column `native_to_botanical_countries`, has a single botanical country. The map
of botanical countries is downloaded from the
[TDWG repository](https://github.com/tdwg/wgsrpd) only once and kept with the
WCVP data. Setting `save = TRUE` writes the map within a subfolder named after
the current date, in any of the formats JPG, PDF, PNG or TIFF.\

```{r, eval = FALSE}
endemicMap(inputdf = fab,
           save = TRUE,
           dir = "results_endemicMap",
           filename = "endemic_map_Fabaceae",
           format = "png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "680px", fig.cap = "FIGURE 1. Number of Fabaceae species endemic to each botanical country."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/endemic_map_Fabaceae.png", dpi = 300)
```

\

About half of the legume species are endemic to a single botanical country.
The richest centres of legume endemism are Western Australia (1,112 endemic
species), the Cape Provinces of South Africa (825) and Iran (731), followed by
Madagascar, Turkey and eastern Brazil.\

\

# 3. Choosing the classes of the map

The classes of endemic species are set with the argument `breaks`, which gives
the upper limit of each class. Botanical countries without endemics are always
shown in their own class, and so are those with more endemics than the last
limit. For a small family such as Lecythidaceae, with about 400 species,
narrower classes give a more informative map. The legend title can be changed
with `leg_title`.\

```{r, eval = FALSE}
lecy <- powoSpecies(family = "Lecythidaceae",
                    verbose = FALSE)

endemicMap(inputdf = lecy,
           breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 20),
           leg_title = "Endemic species",
           save = TRUE,
           dir = "results_endemicMap",
           filename = "endemic_map_Lecythidaceae",
           format = "png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "680px", fig.cap = "FIGURE 2. Number of Lecythidaceae species endemic to each botanical country, with custom classes."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/endemic_map_Lecythidaceae.png", dpi = 300)
```

\

The Brazil nut family has its main centre of endemism in Amazonia and the
northern Andes (Brazil North, Colombia and Ecuador), with secondary centres in
Madagascar, the Malay Peninsula, Borneo and New Guinea.\

\

# 4. Using the map object

`endemicMap` returns a `ggplot` object, so the map can be customised with any
function of __ggplot2__. The data of the map also has the number of endemic
species of each botanical country in the column `endemics`.\

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p <- endemicMap(fab, verbose = FALSE)

# Botanical countries with most endemic species
top <- p$data[order(-p$data$endemics), c("botanical_country", "endemics")]
head(sf::st_drop_geometry(top))

# Adding a title
p + ggplot2::ggtitle("Endemic legumes of the world")
```

\

# 5. Mapping endemics from other data

Any data frame with one species per row and a column with its native
distribution in botanical countries, separated by commas, can be mapped. Use
the argument `distcol` to set the name of the column with the distribution. When
the input data has synonyms (a `status` column, as in
`powoSpecies(synonyms = TRUE)`), only accepted species are counted.\

\

# 6. Reference

Govaerts, R., E. Nic Lughadha, N. Black, R. Turner, and A. Paton. 2021. The
World Checklist of Vascular Plants, a continuously updated resource for
exploring global plant diversity. Scientific Data 8: 215.
